newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Stanbic sees lower debt provisions in H2.
newsitem.headline: Stanbic sees lower debt provisions in H2.

text.p: South Africa's Standard Bank Investment Corp Ltd (Stanbic) said on Tuesday its debt provisions, which jumped 85 percent in the first half of the year, were expected to return to more normal levels by year end.

Stanbic group chief executive Mike Vosloo said collapsed Pepsi bottler, New Age Beverages (NAB), made up the bulk of the 534 million rand ($114.8 million) interim provision, but that African and London units, as well as instalment sales, had also contributed.
"The bugbear of our first half was the provision for credit balances...Had we not had New Age Beverages we would have expected a more normal increase in debt provisioning," Vosloo told reporters.
However, he added that tight economic conditions, on the back of high interest rates, would continue to spawn bad debts.
"Fundamentally, with conditions in the economy generally, one has the feeling that there may be some more bad debts lurking out there," Vosloo said.

Just three years after it spearheaded Pepsi's high-profile return to South Africa, NAB, which kicked off a South African version of the global cola wars, applied for voluntary liquidation in May this year.

Stanbic earlier released headline earnings for the six months to end June up 15 percent to 693 cents a share -- in the lower part of a 688 and 725 cents range forecast by analysts. The dividend rose 25 percent to 136 cents.
South African financial markets are currently anticipating a a cut in interest rates amid signs that the economic growth and inflationary pressures are slowing.
Vosloo said that the group's Africa operations added to the provisions line for the first time, although they were performing well and contributed less than 10 percent of total bad debts.
Stanbic is represented in 14 African countries and is currently eyeing opportunities in Malawi and Angola, although recent renewed political instability in the latter was of concern.
